question: For personal use of campaign funds by state and local candidates in each of the 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico, and for federal candidates: (1) which conduct is a crime (the statute and its mental-state requirement, e.g. knowing and willful), and at what amount it becomes a felony; (2) who can refer a case to prosecutors (the regulator, an auditor, anyone) and who prosecutes (attorney general, district attorney, U.S. Attorney); (3) the steps from referral to charge, plea or trial, and sentence, with any statutory deadlines or limitation periods; (4) statutory penalty ranges (fine, restitution, imprisonment, disqualification from office or future candidacy); and (5) real cases per jurisdiction where available: who, year, amount taken, whether repeat conduct, charge, plea or verdict, and sentence actually served.

title: When taking campaign money becomes a crime, who prosecutes it, and what sentence follows
usableAnswer: One row per jurisdiction (plus federal): criminal statute and mental state, felony threshold, referring and prosecuting bodies, procedural steps and limitation period, penalty ranges including disqualification, and real case outcomes. UNKNOWN where no source settles it; no invented probabilities.
whyItMatters: A candidate who keeps taking campaign money after being caught faces only rising civil fines. Whether and when that becomes a prosecution, and what it costs her, is the ceiling of the whole corruption consequence ladder.
